objects.name: Bicycle
objects.kidDefinition: A two-wheeled ride that you move by pushing pedals with your feet.
objects.dateBasis: The pedal-powered boneshaker bicycle develops in France in the 1860s.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Bicycles developed in stages; this range marks the first pedal-powered bicycle era.
objects.funFact: Early pedal bicycles were nicknamed “boneshakers” because their solid wheels made rough roads feel bumpy.

objects.name: Fountain pen
objects.kidDefinition: A pen with a refillable container that feeds ink to its writing tip.
objects.dateBasis: Petrache Poenaru receives an early fountain-pen patent in France.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Fountain pens improved through many patents; this is an early patent milestone.
objects.funFact: A fountain pen carries its own ink instead of dipping into an inkwell each time.

objects.name: Flat-bottom paper bag
objects.kidDefinition: A paper bag that can stand open because it has a flat bottom.
objects.dateBasis: Margaret Knight patents a machine for making flat-bottom paper bags.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This is the machine patent, not the much older history of paper bags made by hand.
objects.funFact: Knight’s machine made useful flat-bottom bags much faster than folding each one by hand.

objects.name: Ballpoint pen
objects.kidDefinition: A pen that rolls a tiny ball across paper to spread ink.
objects.dateBasis: László Bíró develops the modern successful ballpoint pen.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier ball pens existed; this date marks Bíró’s successful modern design.
objects.funFact: Bíró noticed that newspaper ink dried quickly and used that idea for his pen.

objects.name: Bendy straw
objects.kidDefinition: A drinking straw with a bendy section that helps you sip at an angle.
objects.dateBasis: Joseph Friedman receives a patent for his flexible drinking tube.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the bendable straw patent, not the first straight drinking straw.
objects.funFact: Friedman made the bend by wrapping dental floss around a screw inside a straw.

objects.name: Hula hoop
objects.kidDefinition: A light ring you spin around your waist, arms, or legs.
objects.dateBasis: Wham-O launches the modern plastic Hula Hoop.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Hoop play is ancient; this date means the modern mass-market plastic toy.
objects.funFact: The Hula Hoop craze spread so quickly that millions were sold in its first year.

objects.name: Video game
objects.kidDefinition: An electronic game that shows a game world or score on a screen.
objects.dateBasis: Brookhaven’s Tennis for Two demonstrates an early electronic video game.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Video-game history has several early experiments; this is a well-documented public demonstration.
objects.funFact: Tennis for Two used a laboratory oscilloscope as its screen.

objects.name: Cash machine (ATM)
objects.kidDefinition: A machine that lets people get cash and do simple bank tasks.
objects.dateBasis: The first modern cash machine is installed at Barclays in London.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Several inventors and prototypes contributed; this date marks the first public cash machine installation.
objects.funFact: The first ATM was installed outside a bank in London.

objects.name: Email
objects.kidDefinition: A message sent from one computer to another through a network.
objects.dateBasis: Ray Tomlinson sends the first network email between two computers.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier computer messages stayed inside one machine; this date marks network email.
objects.funFact: Tomlinson chose the @ symbol to separate a person from the computer they used.

objects.name: Smartphone
objects.kidDefinition: A pocket-sized phone that can also run apps and connect to the internet.
objects.dateBasis: IBM’s Simon Personal Communicator becomes the first commercially available smartphone.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Smartphone features evolved over time; this date marks the first commercial device commonly recognized as a smartphone.
objects.funFact: The Simon had a touchscreen and could send faxes before modern app stores existed.

objects.name: Thermometer
objects.kidDefinition: A tool that tells you how hot or cold something is.
objects.dateBasis: Liquid-in-glass thermometers become the familiar form of temperature measuring in the 1640s.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Temperature instruments developed in stages; this range marks the move to liquid-in-glass thermometers rather than one single inventor’s date.
objects.funFact: Early thermometers used liquids that rose and fell as the temperature changed.

objects.name: Stethoscope
objects.kidDefinition: A doctor’s listening tool for hearing sounds inside your body, such as your heartbeat.
objects.dateBasis: René Laënnec invents the first stethoscope for listening to the chest.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This is the first clinical stethoscope milestone; later designs added two earpieces and flexible tubing.
objects.funFact: Laënnec’s first stethoscope was a simple wooden tube.

objects.name: Wheel
objects.kidDefinition: A round object that turns to help move things or make machines work.
objects.dateBasis: The wheel appears in the archaeological record by about 3500 BCE.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The exact inventor is unknown and wheels may have developed in more than one place.
objects.funFact: The earliest wheels may have been used for pottery before people put them on carts.

objects.name: Rubber ball
objects.kidDefinition: A bouncy ball made from stretchy natural rubber.
objects.dateBasis: Ancient Mesoamerican peoples played ball games with rubber balls in this period.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This is an early documented rubber ball and sport, not the later vulcanized rubber used in modern balls.
objects.funFact: The Mesoamerican ballgame may be the oldest known ball sport.

objects.name: Paper
objects.kidDefinition: A thin sheet made from plant fibers that people can write or draw on.
objects.dateBasis: Cai Lun is traditionally credited with improving papermaking in Han China around 105 CE.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Papermaking existed before Cai Lun; this date marks a famous documented improvement, not an absolute first sheet.
objects.funFact: Early paper could be made from plant fibers, rags, and old fishing nets.

objects.name: Chess
objects.kidDefinition: A strategy game where two players move pieces across a checkered board.
objects.dateBasis: Chess develops from earlier Indian games by about the sixth century CE.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Chess changed as it traveled; this range describes its early family of games, not the modern rules.
objects.funFact: The queen became the most powerful piece much later than the game’s early beginnings.

objects.name: Magnetic compass
objects.kidDefinition: A tool with a magnetic needle that points roughly north to help people find direction.
objects.dateBasis: Magnetic compasses are documented in China by the Song period.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The compass developed from magnetic experiments and became useful for navigation over time.
objects.funFact: A compass needle does not point to a drawn arrow—it lines up with Earth’s magnetic field.

objects.name: Eyeglasses
objects.kidDefinition: Lenses held in front of your eyes to help you see more clearly.
objects.dateBasis: Wearable eyeglasses appear in late-thirteenth-century Italy.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The exact inventor is unknown; early glasses were held by hand or balanced on the nose.
objects.funFact: The first glasses probably had no earpieces, so they were tricky to keep in place.

objects.name: Movable-type printing press
objects.kidDefinition: A machine that presses inked letters onto paper to make many copies.
objects.dateBasis: Gutenberg develops a European movable-type printing press in the 1440s.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Printing and movable type existed earlier in Asia; this date marks Gutenberg’s European press tradition.
objects.funFact: Movable letters could be rearranged to print a whole new page.

objects.name: Compound microscope
objects.kidDefinition: A tool with lenses that makes tiny things look much bigger.
objects.dateBasis: Compound microscopes are invented by layering spectacle lenses in tubes around 1590–1600.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The first maker is uncertain; compound microscopes developed through several early experiments.
objects.funFact: A microscope can reveal tiny worlds that are invisible to your eyes alone.

objects.name: Milk chocolate bar
objects.kidDefinition: Chocolate made with cocoa and milk that tastes creamy and sweet.
objects.dateBasis: Daniel Peter develops the first successful milk chocolate using condensed milk.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Chocolate drinks and dark chocolate are much older; this date marks the modern milk-chocolate bar tradition.
objects.funFact: Milk chocolate became possible when condensed milk was mixed with cocoa.

objects.name: Ice-cream cone
objects.kidDefinition: A crisp edible cone that holds a scoop of ice cream.
objects.dateBasis: The modern ice-cream cone becomes popular at the 1904 St. Louis World’s Fair.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier edible pastry containers existed; this date marks the modern cone’s popular breakthrough.
objects.funFact: The cone became famous when ice-cream sellers and waffle makers helped each other at a busy fair.

objects.name: Instant noodles
objects.kidDefinition: Noodles that cook quickly once you add hot water.
objects.dateBasis: Momofuku Ando launches the first packaged instant ramen.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Noodle dishes are ancient; this date means the modern quick-cooking packaged product.
objects.funFact: The first instant noodles were fried so they could dry and cook quickly on the shelf.

objects.name: Cheetos
objects.kidDefinition: Crunchy corn snacks covered in cheesy seasoning.
objects.dateBasis: The Frito Company introduces Cheetos as a cheese-flavored corn snack.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date refers to the launch of the Cheetos brand, not the invention of cheese snacks in general.
objects.funFact: The original snack was made from puffed corn and a cheese coating.

objects.name: McDonald’s fast-food system
objects.kidDefinition: A fast-food restaurant system built around quickly serving familiar meals.
objects.dateBasis: The McDonald brothers reopen with a streamlined self-service restaurant system in San Bernardino.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The first McDonald’s restaurant opened earlier; this date marks the modern Speedee Service system.
objects.funFact: The brothers simplified the menu so food could be prepared and served much faster.

objects.name: Post-it Note
objects.kidDefinition: A small paper note with a light sticky strip that can be moved around.
objects.dateBasis: 3M test-markets the first Post-it Notes after an accidental low-tack adhesive discovery.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The adhesive was discovered earlier; this date marks the product’s test-market launch.
objects.funFact: The first notes were yellow because that was the scrap paper available in the lab.

objects.name: QR code
objects.kidDefinition: A square pattern that a phone camera can scan to open information.
objects.dateBasis: DENSO WAVE develops the QR code for quickly tracking car parts.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date means the original QR code invention; its use for menus, tickets, and links came later.
objects.funFact: QR stands for “quick response” because the pattern can be scanned quickly.

objects.name: Google Search
objects.kidDefinition: A search tool that helps you find webpages, pictures, maps, and answers online.
objects.dateBasis: Google Inc. is officially founded after its Stanford search project becomes a company.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The search project began earlier as BackRub; this date marks the company’s founding.
objects.funFact: Google’s first server rack was built from colorful LEGO bricks.

objects.name: Emoji
objects.kidDefinition: A tiny picture used in a message to show an idea or feeling.
objects.dateBasis: Shigetaka Kurita and NTT DOCOMO develop an early set of mobile emojis.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier smileys and pictograms existed; this date marks an early mobile emoji set.
objects.funFact: Kurita’s original set contained 176 tiny pictures.

objects.name: Netflix DVD service
objects.kidDefinition: A service that lets people choose movies to have delivered or streamed at home.
objects.dateBasis: Netflix launches as a DVD-by-mail rental service.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Streaming arrived later; this date marks Netflix’s original DVD service.
objects.funFact: The first Netflix business sent DVDs through the mail instead of using video stores.

objects.name: YouTube
objects.kidDefinition: A website where people can watch and share videos.
objects.dateBasis: YouTube is founded and its domain is registered in February 2005.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the service’s launch, not the invention of online video itself.
objects.funFact: YouTube began as a place for anyone with a camera and internet connection to share a story.

objects.name: Modern baseball
objects.kidDefinition: A bat-and-ball game where players run around four bases.
objects.dateBasis: The Knickerbocker rules help establish the modern game of baseball.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Bat-and-ball games are much older; this date marks an early modern rule set.
objects.funFact: The four-base diamond made baseball easier for teams to play by the same rules.

objects.name: Modern guitar
objects.kidDefinition: A stringed instrument played by plucking or strumming its strings.
objects.dateBasis: The familiar six-string Spanish guitar form takes shape in the nineteenth century.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Guitar-like instruments are ancient; this date means the recognizable modern form.
objects.funFact: The guitar’s hollow body helps its strings make a louder sound.

objects.name: Safety elevator
objects.kidDefinition: A powered box that carries people up and down between floors.
objects.dateBasis: Elisha Otis demonstrates a safety elevator brake at the 1853 New York World’s Fair.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Lifting platforms existed earlier; this date marks the safety system that made passenger elevators practical.
objects.funFact: Otis’s safety brake was designed to stop the platform if its lifting rope broke.

objects.name: Modern soccer
objects.kidDefinition: A team game where players kick a ball and try to score in a goal.
objects.dateBasis: The Football Association writes down rules for modern association football in England.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Ball-kicking games are ancient; this date marks the organized rules for modern soccer.
objects.funFact: The word soccer comes from “association,” the organization that set the rules.

objects.name: Modern lawn tennis
objects.kidDefinition: A racket game where players hit a ball over a net.
objects.dateBasis: Walter Wingfield patents and markets the modern lawn-tennis game.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Older racket games existed; this date marks the lawn version that led to today’s tennis.
objects.funFact: Early lawn tennis was played on an hourglass-shaped court.

objects.name: Modern American football
objects.kidDefinition: A team game where players run or pass an oval ball toward an end zone.
objects.dateBasis: Walter Camp’s rule changes help create the modern American football game.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Rugby and other football codes came earlier; this date means the American game’s modern rules.
objects.funFact: The line of scrimmage and downs helped turn football into a play-by-play strategy game.

objects.name: Basketball
objects.kidDefinition: A team game where players bounce a ball and shoot it through a high hoop.
objects.dateBasis: James Naismith invents basketball for an indoor winter activity.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks Naismith’s first rules, while the game’s equipment and rules changed later.
objects.funFact: The first basket was a peach basket, so someone had to retrieve the ball after every score.

objects.name: Modern escalator
objects.kidDefinition: A moving staircase that carries people up or down.
objects.dateBasis: Jesse Reno patents an inclined moving stairway, an early modern escalator design.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Moving walkways and stair ideas came earlier; this date marks the continuous-step design’s early patent era.
objects.funFact: An escalator lets a crowd move between floors without everyone climbing at once.

objects.name: Electronic television
objects.kidDefinition: A screen that receives moving pictures and sound for people to watch.
objects.dateBasis: Philo Farnsworth demonstrates an all-electronic television system.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Mechanical television experiments came earlier; this date marks the electronic system behind modern TV.
objects.funFact: The first image Farnsworth transmitted was a simple line and shape, not a full show.

objects.name: Digital clock
objects.kidDefinition: A clock that shows the time with glowing or printed numbers.
objects.dateBasis: The first fully electronic digital clock is demonstrated by the D.E. Protzmann company.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Digital time displays developed through several experiments; this date marks an early electronic clock product.
objects.funFact: Digital clocks show time as numbers instead of moving hands around a face.

objects.name: Remote-control car
objects.kidDefinition: A small toy car steered from a distance with a handheld controller.
objects.dateBasis: Commercial radio-controlled model cars become popular in the 1960s.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Radio control was demonstrated earlier; this date means the familiar toy-car era.
objects.funFact: The controller sends radio signals that tell the toy’s motor which way to turn.

objects.name: Camera drone
objects.kidDefinition: A flying machine that can be steered from the ground, often with a camera.
objects.dateBasis: Easy-to-fly camera drones become widely available to families and hobbyists in the 2010s.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Pilotless aircraft are much older; this date means the small consumer camera-drone form children recognize.
objects.funFact: A drone’s spinning propellers let it hover, rise, and move in several directions.

objects.name: Monopoly
objects.kidDefinition: A board game about buying streets, building houses, and collecting rent.
objects.dateBasis: Parker Brothers publishes Monopoly in the form that becomes a worldwide classic.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The game grew from earlier land-trading games; this date marks the familiar commercial edition.
objects.funFact: Monopoly’s longest game can last for hours because players keep trading and building.

objects.name: Scrabble
objects.kidDefinition: A word game where players build words from letter tiles on a board.
objects.dateBasis: The Scrabble name and commercial game begin in the late 1940s.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Alfred Mosher Butts designed an earlier version called Lexiko and Criss-Crosswords.
objects.funFact: Letter tiles are worth different points, so a short unusual word can be a big score.

objects.name: Operation
objects.kidDefinition: A buzzer game where players remove silly body parts with tweezers.
objects.dateBasis: Milton Bradley publishes Operation as a commercial board game.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The game began as a college design; this date marks its mass-market release.
objects.funFact: The metal tweezers complete a circuit, so touching the sides makes the patient’s nose light up.

objects.name: Battleship
objects.kidDefinition: A guessing game where players try to find hidden ships on a grid.
objects.dateBasis: Milton Bradley releases the familiar plastic-grid Battleship board game.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Paper naval guessing games existed earlier; this date marks the classic boxed edition.
objects.funFact: Players call out coordinates such as B-4 to search the other player’s hidden fleet.

objects.name: UNO
objects.kidDefinition: A fast card game where players match colors and numbers and try to empty their hand.
objects.dateBasis: Merle Robbins creates and begins selling UNO in Reading, Ohio.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Card games are much older; this date marks the creation of the UNO game.
objects.funFact: The name UNO means “one,” which players shout when they have one card left.

objects.name: Connect 4
objects.kidDefinition: A drop-four game where players try to line up four counters in a row.
objects.dateBasis: Milton Bradley launches Connect 4 as a vertical four-in-a-row game.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Four-in-a-row puzzles existed earlier; this date marks the familiar upright commercial game.
objects.funFact: The upright frame makes players think in three directions: across, up and down, and diagonally.

objects.name: Jenga
objects.kidDefinition: A stacking game where players pull wooden blocks and place them on top.
objects.dateBasis: Leslie Scott introduces Jenga at the London Toy Fair.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Stacking-block games are older; this date marks the Jenga brand and rules.
objects.funFact: Jenga comes from a Swahili word meaning “to build.”

objects.name: Catan
objects.kidDefinition: A strategy game where players trade resources and build roads, towns, and cities.
objects.dateBasis: Klaus Teuber’s Die Siedler von Catan is first published in Germany.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The English title Catan arrived later; this date marks the original game’s publication.
objects.funFact: Catan’s board changes between games because its island tiles can be arranged in new patterns.

objects.name: Roller skates
objects.kidDefinition: Shoes with wheels that let you roll along the ground.
objects.dateBasis: James Plimpton patents a practical four-wheel roller skate design.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier skates existed; this date marks the design that made turning and balancing much easier.
objects.funFact: Plimpton’s four wheels could tilt, helping skaters turn instead of rolling only in a straight line.

objects.name: Modern roller coaster
objects.kidDefinition: A track ride with hills, drops, and turns that carries cars full of riders.
objects.dateBasis: LaMarcus Thompson opens the Switchback Railway at Coney Island, an early modern roller coaster.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Gravity rides existed earlier; this date marks the amusement-park roller-coaster era.
objects.funFact: The first riders paid a nickel to travel along a short, bumpy track.

objects.name: Pogo stick
objects.kidDefinition: A springy stick with footrests that lets you bounce up and down.
objects.dateBasis: The Pogo Stick is patented by George Hansburg after the first German spring-jumping stick designs.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Spring-jumping devices came earlier; this date marks the named toy’s patent era.
objects.funFact: The pogo stick’s spring stores your downward push and sends you back up.

objects.name: Band-Aid adhesive bandage
objects.kidDefinition: A small sticky strip with a soft pad that covers a little cut or scrape.
objects.dateBasis: Johnson & Johnson introduces the Band-Aid brand adhesive bandage after its 1920 invention.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Adhesive dressings existed earlier; this date marks the familiar ready-to-use home bandage.
objects.funFact: The first Band-Aids were made by hand and were much longer than today’s small strips.

objects.name: Skateboard
objects.kidDefinition: A narrow board with four wheels that people ride by balancing and pushing.
objects.dateBasis: The modern skateboard grows from homemade sidewalk scooters and becomes a commercial youth product in the late 1950s.
objects.ambiguityNotes: People built early boards from roller-skate wheels; this date means the recognizable skateboard era.
objects.funFact: Early skateboards were sometimes called sidewalk surfers because riders copied surfing moves.

objects.name: Barbie
objects.kidDefinition: A fashion doll and story world where children can imagine many different lives and jobs.
objects.dateBasis: Ruth Handler introduces Barbie at the New York Toy Fair.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Dolls are ancient; this date marks the first Barbie doll and brand.
objects.funFact: Barbie’s first outfit was a black-and-white striped swimsuit.

objects.name: Sesame Street
objects.kidDefinition: A children’s TV show where friendly characters explore words, numbers, music, and feelings.
objects.dateBasis: Sesame Street premieres on public television in the United States.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Children’s television came earlier; this date marks the premiere of the Sesame Street series.
objects.funFact: The show was designed with educators so its songs and stories could teach while entertaining.

objects.name: Super Mario
objects.kidDefinition: A video-game hero who runs, jumps, and explores colorful worlds.
objects.dateBasis: Super Mario Bros. launches for the Nintendo Entertainment System.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Mario appeared in earlier arcade games; this date marks the famous Super Mario Bros. adventure.
objects.funFact: Mario’s famous mustache helped him look clear on early low-resolution game screens.

objects.name: Pac-Man
objects.kidDefinition: A yellow arcade character who eats dots, avoids ghosts, and explores a maze.
objects.dateBasis: Namco releases the first Pac-Man arcade game in Japan.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the original arcade game and character, before later home versions and sequels.
objects.funFact: Pac-Man was designed as a friendly character for a wider audience, including people who did not usually play arcade games.

objects.name: Sonic the Hedgehog
objects.kidDefinition: A super-fast blue game character who races through bright worlds and collects rings.
objects.dateBasis: Sega releases the first Sonic the Hedgehog game for the Mega Drive/Genesis.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Sonic’s character and games expanded later; this date marks the original platform game.
objects.funFact: Sonic’s bright blue color was chosen to match Sega’s logo and make him easy to recognize.

objects.name: Pokémon
objects.kidDefinition: A world of creature-catching adventures, games, shows, cards, and stories.
objects.dateBasis: Pokémon Red and Green launch in Japan for the Game Boy.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The franchise spread worldwide in later years; this date marks the first Pokémon games.
objects.funFact: The name Pokémon is short for “Pocket Monsters.”

objects.name: Harry Potter
objects.kidDefinition: A fantasy story about a young wizard learning magic and friendship at school.
objects.dateBasis: Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone is first published in the United Kingdom.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the first book, before the film series and later Wizarding World stories.
objects.funFact: The first book was published with a different title, Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone, in the United States.

objects.name: Peppa Pig
objects.kidDefinition: An animated piglet who explores family life, play, and muddy puddles.
objects.dateBasis: Peppa Pig first airs in the United Kingdom.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the television series premiere, not later books, toys, or films.
objects.funFact: Peppa’s favorite outdoor activity is jumping in muddy puddles.

objects.name: Minecraft
objects.kidDefinition: A game where players explore, build, craft, and create stories from blocks.
objects.dateBasis: Minecraft reaches its full official release after years of development.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Early playable versions appeared earlier; this date marks the full release.
objects.funFact: Minecraft worlds are made from blocks, but players can build almost anything with them.

objects.name: Bluey
objects.kidDefinition: An animated blue heeler puppy who learns through imaginative play with family and friends.
objects.dateBasis: Bluey premieres on ABC Kids in Australia.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the television series premiere and its first episodes.
objects.funFact: Bluey’s games often turn ordinary family moments into make-believe adventures.

objects.name: Electric refrigerator
objects.kidDefinition: A powered kitchen cabinet that keeps food and drinks cold.
objects.dateBasis: The first practical electric household refrigerators begin appearing in homes in the 1910s.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Iceboxes and experimental cooling machines came earlier; this date marks the modern electric home appliance.
objects.funFact: A refrigerator moves heat out of its inside space, making the food area cold.

objects.name: Pop-up toaster
objects.kidDefinition: A small kitchen appliance that browns slices of bread with hot electric wires.
objects.dateBasis: The first commercially successful automatic pop-up toaster is introduced by Toastmaster.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier electric bread toasters existed; this date marks the automatic pop-up form familiar today.
objects.funFact: A pop-up toaster uses a timer and a spring to lift toast when it is ready.

objects.name: Jacuzzi whirlpool tub
objects.kidDefinition: A warm tub with jets that push bubbles and water around you.
objects.dateBasis: The Jacuzzi family introduces the first built-in whirlpool bath for home use.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The Jacuzzi name is a brand; this date marks the home whirlpool tub that made the name familiar.
objects.funFact: The water jets are made by mixing moving water with air to create the bubbly massage.

objects.name: Modern zipper
objects.kidDefinition: A row of teeth joined by a slider to close clothes, bags, or jackets.
objects.dateBasis: Gideon Sundback patents the “Separate Fastener,” the modern zipper design.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier fasteners existed; this date marks the tooth-and-slider design used today.
objects.funFact: The word zipper became popular after the fastener was used on rubber boots.

objects.name: Safety pin
objects.kidDefinition: A bent piece of wire with a clasp that keeps the sharp point covered.
objects.dateBasis: Walter Hunt patents the modern safety pin.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Pins and brooches are ancient; this date marks Hunt’s springy covered-point design.
objects.funFact: The clasp protects fingers from the pin’s sharp point while holding fabric together.

objects.name: Powered vacuum cleaner
objects.kidDefinition: A machine that uses moving air to suck up dust and crumbs.
objects.dateBasis: Hubert Cecil Booth demonstrates a powered vacuum-cleaning machine in London.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Manual carpet sweepers came earlier; this date marks the powered suction-cleaner era.
objects.funFact: Booth tested the idea by seeing whether a handkerchief could stop dust from reaching his mouth.

objects.name: Electric hair dryer
objects.kidDefinition: A handheld appliance that blows warm air to dry hair.
objects.dateBasis: Handheld electric hair dryers become available in the 1920s.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Salon drying machines existed earlier; this date means the portable household form.
objects.funFact: Early hair dryers were heavy because their motors were adapted from vacuum cleaners.

objects.name: Disposable diaper
objects.kidDefinition: A ready-to-use diaper designed to be thrown away once it is soiled.
objects.dateBasis: Pampers disposable diapers begin commercial production.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Cloth diapers are much older; this date marks the widely distributed disposable diaper product.
objects.funFact: Early disposable diapers were tested with paper, plastic, and absorbent wood pulp.

objects.name: UPC barcode
objects.kidDefinition: A pattern of lines that stores can scan to identify a product and its price.
objects.dateBasis: The first retail UPC barcode is scanned on a pack of Wrigley’s gum.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Barcode ideas and patents came earlier; this date marks the first ordinary supermarket scan.
objects.funFact: The first scanned product was a pack of chewing gum bought in Ohio.

objects.name: Pocket calculator
objects.kidDefinition: A small battery-powered device that does math with buttons and a screen.
objects.dateBasis: The HP-35 becomes the first pocket-sized scientific calculator.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Large mechanical and electronic calculators came earlier; this date marks the pocket form.
objects.funFact: The HP-35 was named for its 35 keys, not for the number of calculations it could do.

objects.name: Laptop computer
objects.kidDefinition: A portable computer with a screen, keyboard, and battery in one folding case.
objects.dateBasis: The Osborne 1 launches as an early commercially successful portable computer.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Portable computers existed as prototypes and specialized machines earlier; this date marks the early laptop category.
objects.funFact: The Osborne 1 was portable, but it weighed about 11 kilograms—more like a small suitcase than a school laptop.

objects.name: Pocket lighter
objects.kidDefinition: A small tool that makes a flame for lighting a candle, campfire, or stove.
objects.dateBasis: Johann Wolfgang Döbereiner develops the first practical pocket lighter, the Döbereiner lamp.
objects.ambiguityNotes: People made flames in many ways earlier; this date marks a portable chemical lighter.
objects.funFact: The first pocket lighter used hydrogen gas and a spark-making platinum catalyst.

objects.name: Safety match
objects.kidDefinition: A small wooden stick that lights when rubbed on a special striking surface.
objects.dateBasis: Gustaf Erik Pasch develops a safer match using a separate striking surface.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Friction matches existed earlier; this date marks the safer design used by modern matchboxes.
objects.funFact: Keeping the reactive chemicals separate made safety matches much less likely to ignite by accident.

objects.name: Handheld flashlight
objects.kidDefinition: A battery-powered lamp that sends a beam of light where you point it.
objects.dateBasis: The first practical battery-powered handheld flashlight is patented and sold by the American Ever Ready Company.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Electric lamps and batteries came earlier; this date marks the familiar handheld torch form.
objects.funFact: Early flashlights were called electric torches because their batteries did not shine continuously for long.

objects.name: Corrugated cardboard
objects.kidDefinition: Strong paperboard made with a wavy layer inside, often used for boxes.
objects.dateBasis: The first U.S. patent for corrugated paperboard helps establish the modern shipping box material.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Flat paperboard is older; this date marks the ridged material used in cardboard boxes.
objects.funFact: The wavy middle layer acts like tiny springs, making a box stronger without making it solid and heavy.

objects.name: Paper clip
objects.kidDefinition: A bent piece of wire that holds sheets of paper together without glue.
objects.dateBasis: The Gem paper clip design is patented in the United States.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Many wire fasteners came earlier; this date marks the familiar looped paper-clip form.
objects.funFact: A paper clip holds pages by squeezing them together with the springiness of its bent wire.

objects.name: Office stapler
objects.kidDefinition: A tool that pushes small metal staples through paper to hold pages together.
objects.dateBasis: The first practical modern stapler is patented for fastening sheets of paper.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier machines fastened books and upholstery; this date marks the small office tool.
objects.funFact: A stapler bends the two little metal legs under the paper so the pages stay together.

objects.name: Cellophane tape
objects.kidDefinition: A clear sticky strip used to join, repair, or wrap things.
objects.dateBasis: 3M develops and markets transparent cellophane tape, later known as Scotch tape.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Adhesive tapes existed earlier; this date marks the clear household tape form.
objects.funFact: The first clear tape was made to help seal packages without hiding the label underneath.

objects.name: Hot glue gun
objects.kidDefinition: A tool that melts glue sticks so you can join craft materials together.
objects.dateBasis: The first commercial hot-melt glue gun is developed for sealing and craft-like repairs.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Hot-melt adhesives existed earlier; this date marks the handheld glue-gun form.
objects.funFact: The glue is solid in the stick but becomes runny when the gun warms it up.

objects.name: Felt-tip marker
objects.kidDefinition: A pen with a porous tip that lays down a bold line of ink.
objects.dateBasis: The modern felt-tip marker is introduced commercially in Japan and then spreads worldwide.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Pens with porous tips existed earlier; this date marks the familiar marker-pen product.
objects.funFact: The marker’s tip works like a tiny bundle of fibers that carries ink to the page.

objects.name: Super glue
objects.kidDefinition: A fast-setting liquid glue that bonds many hard surfaces together.
objects.dateBasis: Cyanoacrylate adhesive is commercialized as Super Glue.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The adhesive was discovered earlier; this date marks the consumer super-glue product.
objects.funFact: A tiny amount of moisture on a surface helps super glue harden quickly.

objects.name: Lawnmower
objects.kidDefinition: A machine with blades that trims grass to keep a lawn neat.
objects.dateBasis: Edwin Budding patents a push reel lawnmower in England.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Grass-cutting tools existed earlier; this date marks the first practical lawnmower design.
objects.funFact: The first lawnmower was inspired by a machine that trimmed the fuzzy surface of cloth.

objects.name: Electric fan
objects.kidDefinition: A machine with spinning blades that moves air to help people feel cooler.
objects.dateBasis: Schuyler Wheeler develops one of the first practical electric fans.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Hand fans and wind-powered devices are much older; this date marks the electric room fan.
objects.funFact: An electric fan cools people by moving air across their skin rather than making the room much colder.

objects.name: Home stereo
objects.kidDefinition: A sound system that uses separate speakers to make music feel wider and more surrounding.
objects.dateBasis: Early two-channel stereo sound systems are demonstrated for recorded music and film.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Sound recording is older; this date marks the two-channel stereo experience.
objects.funFact: Stereo sends slightly different sounds to each speaker so your ears can sense direction.

objects.name: Electric car
objects.kidDefinition: A car moved by an electric motor and rechargeable batteries instead of a gasoline engine.
objects.dateBasis: William Morrison builds an early practical electric automobile in the United States.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Electric car experiments began earlier; this date marks an early road-going passenger car.
objects.funFact: Early electric cars were quiet and simple to drive, but batteries limited how far they could travel.

objects.name: Liquid-fueled rocket
objects.kidDefinition: A powered vehicle that blasts upward by shooting hot gases downward.
objects.dateBasis: Robert Goddard launches the first liquid-fueled rocket.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Solid rockets and fireworks are much older; this date marks the liquid-fueled rocket path to spaceflight.
objects.funFact: Goddard’s first liquid-fueled rocket flew for only about two and a half seconds.

objects.name: Silicon solar panel
objects.kidDefinition: A panel that turns sunlight into electricity.
objects.dateBasis: Bell Labs demonstrates the first practical silicon solar cell.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The photovoltaic effect was discovered earlier; this date marks a useful practical solar cell.
objects.funFact: A solar panel makes electricity when light gives energy to tiny particles inside silicon.

objects.name: Popcorn
objects.kidDefinition: A snack made when dry corn kernels pop into fluffy white pieces.
objects.dateBasis: Archaeologists found ancient popcorn-like corn remains in Peru.
objects.ambiguityNotes: People have popped corn for thousands of years; the exact first batch is unknown.
objects.funFact: Some ancient people in Peru were eating popped corn thousands of years ago.

objects.name: Hot chocolate
objects.kidDefinition: A warm, sweet drink made with cocoa or chocolate and milk or water.
objects.dateBasis: Mesoamerican peoples prepare early cacao drinks long before modern sweet hot chocolate.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Early cacao drinks were often bitter and spiced; this date marks the long cacao-drink tradition.
objects.funFact: Early cacao drinks were often frothy, spicy, and not sweet like a modern mug of cocoa.

objects.name: Marshmallow candy
objects.kidDefinition: A soft, bouncy candy that can be toasted, melted, or eaten plain.
objects.dateBasis: French confectioners develop the whipped commercial marshmallow candy from the older mallow-root treat.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The mallow plant was used much earlier; this date marks the modern whipped candy.
objects.funFact: Modern marshmallows use whipped sugar and gelatin instead of mallow plant sap.

objects.name: Potato chips
objects.kidDefinition: Thin slices of potato fried or baked until they become crisp.
objects.dateBasis: The famous Saratoga Springs story places an early restaurant-style potato chip in the 1850s.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The exact origin story is debated; this date marks the early commercial potato-chip tradition.
objects.funFact: Thin potato slices became a clever answer to a diner who complained that his fried potatoes were too thick.

objects.name: Can opener
objects.kidDefinition: A tool that cuts through a metal can so you can reach the food inside.
objects.dateBasis: The first dedicated handheld can openers are patented after canned food had already existed for decades.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Early tins were opened with knives, hammers, or chisels; this date marks the dedicated kitchen tool.
objects.funFact: Canned food was sold long before the can opener, so opening a tin could require a hammer and chisel.

objects.name: Tea bag
objects.kidDefinition: A small porous bag that holds tea leaves while they steep in hot water.
objects.dateBasis: Tea importer Thomas Sullivan’s sample bags inspire the modern tea-bag habit.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Early bags were silk and not always intended to be steeped; this date marks the accidental modern use.
objects.funFact: Tea bags became popular after customers accidentally steeped the sample bags instead of emptying them.

objects.name: Sliced bread
objects.kidDefinition: A loaf cut into even slices so sandwiches and toast are quick to make.
objects.dateBasis: Otto Rohwedder’s bread-slicing machine helps launch commercially sliced bread.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Bread is ancient; this date marks the machine-sliced packaged loaf.
objects.funFact: Machine-sliced bread was advertised as a way to make every slice the same thickness.

objects.name: Bar soap
objects.kidDefinition: A cleaning bar that mixes with water to help wash dirt and germs away.
objects.dateBasis: Ancient Mesopotamian recipes describe soap-like mixtures made from fats and alkaline ash.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Cleaning mixtures developed in several places; this date marks very early soap-making evidence.
objects.funFact: The earliest soap-like recipes used fats or oils mixed with alkaline ash.

objects.name: Toothpaste
objects.kidDefinition: A paste or gel used with a toothbrush to clean teeth.
objects.dateBasis: Colgate begins selling toothpaste in jars, helping create the modern commercial toothpaste product.
objects.ambiguityNotes: People cleaned teeth with powders and twigs much earlier; this date marks the commercial paste era.
objects.funFact: Early commercial toothpaste was sold in jars before collapsible tubes became common.

objects.name: Liquid shampoo
objects.kidDefinition: A liquid cleanser made for washing hair.
objects.dateBasis: The first commercial liquid shampoo products appear in the early twentieth century.
objects.ambiguityNotes: People washed hair with soaps and herbal mixtures earlier; this date marks the modern liquid shampoo product.
objects.funFact: The word shampoo comes from a word meaning to massage or knead.

objects.name: Coca-Cola
objects.kidDefinition: A fizzy cola drink first sold as a flavored soda long ago.
objects.dateBasis: Coca-Cola is first served at Jacobs’ Pharmacy in Atlanta.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Cola flavors and soft drinks changed over time; this date marks the Coca-Cola brand’s beginning.
objects.funFact: The first Coca-Cola was served from a soda fountain, not a can or plastic bottle.

objects.name: Soda can
objects.kidDefinition: A lightweight metal can that holds a fizzy drink and opens with a pull tab.
objects.dateBasis: Metal cans become practical for carbonated soft drinks in the 1950s.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Canned beer came earlier; this date marks the familiar mass-market soda-can era.
objects.funFact: Early soda cans needed a church-key opener before pull tabs were invented.

objects.name: Fanta
objects.kidDefinition: A fizzy fruit-flavored soft drink brand.
objects.dateBasis: Fanta is created in Germany during a Coca-Cola syrup shortage.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The recipe and flavors changed over time; this date marks the brand’s origin.
objects.funFact: The first Fanta was made with ingredients available locally during wartime shortages.

objects.name: Sprite
objects.kidDefinition: A clear, lemon-lime fizzy soft drink.
objects.dateBasis: The Coca-Cola Company introduces Sprite as a lemon-lime soft drink.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Lemon-lime sodas existed earlier; this date marks the Sprite brand.
objects.funFact: Sprite’s name was inspired by a cheerful elf character used in Coca-Cola advertising.

objects.name: Plastic water bottle
objects.kidDefinition: A lightweight plastic bottle made to carry drinking water.
objects.dateBasis: Nathaniel Wyeth patents a strong PET plastic bottle suitable for carbonated drinks and water.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Glass water bottles are older; this date marks the familiar lightweight PET bottle form.
objects.funFact: PET plastic is light, clear, and strong enough to hold fizzy drinks without shattering.

objects.name: Table fork
objects.kidDefinition: A small eating tool with prongs that helps pick up food.
objects.dateBasis: Forks spread into medieval European table settings after earlier use in Byzantium and the Middle East.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Fork-like tools are ancient; this date marks the fork becoming a table utensil in Europe.
objects.funFact: Forks were once considered strange or fancy at European dining tables.

objects.name: Toothbrush
objects.kidDefinition: A small brush used with toothpaste to clean your teeth.
objects.dateBasis: A bristle toothbrush is documented in China during the Ming dynasty.
objects.ambiguityNotes: People cleaned teeth with twigs and cloth earlier; this date marks the bristle-brush form.
objects.funFact: Early Chinese toothbrushes used stiff bristles attached to a handle made from bamboo or bone.

objects.name: Flush toilet
objects.kidDefinition: A toilet that carries waste away with a flow of water.
objects.dateBasis: Sir John Harington describes and builds an early flush toilet for Queen Elizabeth I.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Flush systems existed in ancient civilizations; this date marks an early modern household design.
objects.funFact: Harington gave his flush toilet a playful name: Ajax.

objects.name: Yo-yo
objects.kidDefinition: A toy with two disks and a string that rolls down and back up your hand.
objects.dateBasis: Ancient Greek pottery and objects show yo-yo-like toys in use.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Similar disk-and-string toys may be older; this date marks clear ancient evidence.
objects.funFact: Ancient Greek children may have dedicated yo-yos to the gods when they grew up.

objects.name: Flying disc
objects.kidDefinition: A flat disc that flies when you throw it spinning through the air.
objects.dateBasis: Wham-O begins selling the Pluto Platter, the flying disc that becomes the Frisbee.
objects.ambiguityNotes: People tossed pie tins earlier; this date marks the commercial flying-disc toy.
objects.funFact: The name Frisbee came from college students tossing empty pie plates from the Frisbie Pie Company.

objects.name: Easy-Bake Oven
objects.kidDefinition: A toy oven that lets children bake tiny treats using the heat of a light bulb.
objects.dateBasis: Kenner launches the Easy-Bake Oven.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Toy ovens existed earlier; this date marks the famous light-bulb-powered version.
objects.funFact: The first Easy-Bake Oven used an ordinary light bulb as its tiny heating element.

objects.name: TV remote control
objects.kidDefinition: A handheld controller that changes a television from across the room.
objects.dateBasis: Zenith introduces the Lazy Bones wired television remote control.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Wireless remotes came later; this date marks the first commercial TV remote system.
objects.funFact: The first TV remote was connected to the television by a long wire.

objects.name: Slow cooker
objects.kidDefinition: An electric pot that cooks food gently for several hours.
objects.dateBasis: The Rival Crock-Pot becomes a widely sold household slow cooker.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Slow cooking is ancient; this date marks the electric countertop appliance.
objects.funFact: A slow cooker can turn a few simple ingredients into a warm meal while nobody stirs a pot.

objects.name: Portable cassette player
objects.kidDefinition: A small player that lets one person listen to music through headphones while walking around.
objects.dateBasis: Sony launches the TPS-L2 Walkman portable cassette player.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Portable radios existed earlier; this date marks the personal music player made for headphones.
objects.funFact: The first Walkman came with two headphone jacks so two people could listen together.

objects.name: Instant camera
objects.kidDefinition: A camera that develops a physical photo quickly when you take the picture.
objects.dateBasis: Edwin Land’s Land Camera Model 95 becomes the first successful Polaroid instant camera.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Cameras and photographic film are older; this date marks the one-minute instant-photo experience.
objects.funFact: The first Polaroid camera made a finished black-and-white photo in about a minute.

objects.name: Photocopier
objects.kidDefinition: A machine that makes a paper copy of a page or picture.
objects.dateBasis: Xerox introduces the Xerox 914, the first successful plain-paper office copier.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Copying machines existed earlier; this date marks the modern office photocopier.
objects.funFact: The Xerox 914 was so useful that some early machines were leased instead of sold.

objects.name: Document scanner
objects.kidDefinition: A device that turns a paper picture or page into a digital image.
objects.dateBasis: Russell Kirsch’s drum scanner creates one of the first digital image scans.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Image scanning developed through several laboratory machines; this date marks an early digital scan.
objects.funFact: The first scanned picture was a small, blurry black-and-white image of Kirsch’s baby son.

objects.name: Computer printer
objects.kidDefinition: A machine that puts words or pictures from a computer onto paper.
objects.dateBasis: The Xerox laser printer project demonstrates the path to modern computer printing.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Printers and plotters existed earlier; this date marks the computer-connected office printer era.
objects.funFact: Laser printers use tiny dots of toner to build letters and pictures on a page.

objects.name: 3D printer
objects.kidDefinition: A machine that builds a solid object one thin layer at a time.
objects.dateBasis: Chuck Hull develops stereolithography, an early 3D-printing process.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Prototypes and related ideas came earlier; this date marks the first practical stereolithography process.
objects.funFact: A 3D printer can make a shape with layers so thin they look like one smooth object.

objects.name: Play-Doh
objects.kidDefinition: Soft, colorful modeling compound that children can shape into pretend creations.
objects.dateBasis: Play-Doh is introduced as a children’s modeling compound after beginning as a wallpaper cleaner.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Modeling clays are older; this date marks the Play-Doh product and brand.
objects.funFact: Play-Doh began as a way to clean soot from wallpaper before children turned it into a toy.

objects.name: Chutes and Ladders
objects.kidDefinition: A board game where players climb ladders and slide down chutes on the way to the finish.
objects.dateBasis: Milton Bradley publishes the familiar American Chutes and Ladders edition.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The game has much older Indian roots; this date marks the modern American children’s edition.
objects.funFact: The game’s older Indian ancestor used snakes and ladders to teach ideas about good and bad choices.

objects.name: Exercise treadmill
objects.kidDefinition: A moving belt that lets someone walk or run while staying in one place.
objects.dateBasis: Robert Bruce and Wayne Quinton develop a modern medical exercise treadmill.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Treadwheel machines were used for work and punishment earlier; this date marks the exercise-testing treadmill.
objects.funFact: Doctors used early treadmills to study how a person’s heart responds to exercise.

objects.name: Elliptical trainer
objects.kidDefinition: An exercise machine with foot pedals that glide in a smooth oval path.
objects.dateBasis: Precor introduces the Elliptical Fitness Crosstrainer for low-impact exercise.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Elliptical motion is older; this date marks the recognizable gym machine.
objects.funFact: The elliptical motion lets feet stay on the pedals while arms and legs move together.

objects.name: Electric traffic light
objects.kidDefinition: A road signal that uses colored lights to tell drivers and walkers when to stop or go.
objects.dateBasis: The first electric traffic signal with red and green lights is installed in Cleveland.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Gas-lit and manually operated signals came earlier; this date marks the electric road signal.
objects.funFact: Early electric traffic lights used only red and green; yellow was added later.

objects.name: Motorized fire engine
objects.kidDefinition: A vehicle that carries firefighters, hoses, ladders, and water to a fire.
objects.dateBasis: Motorized fire engines begin replacing horse-drawn engines in city fire departments.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Firefighting vehicles and horse-drawn engines are older; this date marks the motorized form.
objects.funFact: Early motorized fire engines were sometimes converted from cars or trucks.

objects.name: Motor ambulance
objects.kidDefinition: A vehicle that carries sick or injured people to medical care.
objects.dateBasis: The first motor ambulances begin service in major cities at the end of the nineteenth century.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Horse-drawn ambulance services came earlier; this date marks the motorized emergency vehicle.
objects.funFact: Early motor ambulances were adapted from electric cars and could carry a patient lying down.

objects.name: Aluminum foil
objects.kidDefinition: A thin, shiny metal sheet used to wrap and cover food.
objects.dateBasis: Commercial aluminum foil production begins in Switzerland.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Tin foil came earlier; this date marks the lightweight aluminum kitchen foil people use today.
objects.funFact: Aluminum foil replaced tin foil because it was lighter and did not leave a metallic taste.

objects.name: Modern helicopter
objects.kidDefinition: An aircraft with spinning blades that can lift straight up and hover.
objects.dateBasis: The Sikorsky R-4 becomes the first mass-produced practical helicopter.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier rotorcraft flew experimentally; this date marks the practical helicopter era.
objects.funFact: A helicopter can hover because its rotor pushes air downward while the aircraft stays in place.

objects.name: Powered submarine
objects.kidDefinition: A boat designed to travel underwater for long periods.
objects.dateBasis: The USS Holland becomes an early practical powered submarine for a navy.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Submersible ideas and hand-powered boats came earlier; this date marks the practical powered submarine.
objects.funFact: Submarines control their depth by taking water into or pushing water out of ballast tanks.

objects.name: Popsicle
objects.kidDefinition: A frozen sweet treat on a stick.
objects.dateBasis: Frank Epperson begins selling his frozen “Epsicle,” later called the Popsicle.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Frozen desserts are older; this date marks the branded stick-shaped treat.
objects.funFact: The idea began when a drink with a stirring stick froze outside overnight.

objects.name: Tomato ketchup
objects.kidDefinition: A thick, sweet-tangy tomato sauce used on fries, burgers, and more.
objects.dateBasis: H.J. Heinz begins selling the familiar bottled tomato ketchup.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Ketchup sauces have older Asian roots; this date marks the modern tomato condiment.
objects.funFact: Early ketchup recipes used ingredients such as mushrooms, walnuts, or fish before tomato ketchup won out.

objects.name: Modern chewing gum
objects.kidDefinition: A stretchy candy you chew for flavor without swallowing it.
objects.dateBasis: William Finley Semple patents a modern chewing-gum formula.
objects.ambiguityNotes: People chewed natural resins much earlier; this date marks the modern gum product.
objects.funFact: Chewing gum bubbles work because the gum base stretches around air.

objects.name: Chicken nuggets
objects.kidDefinition: Small breaded pieces of chicken made for dipping and easy eating.
objects.dateBasis: McDonald’s introduces Chicken McNuggets nationwide in the United States.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Breaded chicken is older; this date marks the familiar fast-food nugget format.
objects.funFact: The nugget shape was designed to make the pieces easy to dip and share.

objects.name: Highlighter pen
objects.kidDefinition: A bright marker used to make important words stand out on a page.
objects.dateBasis: The modern fluorescent highlighter pen is introduced for marking text.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Colored pencils and markers came earlier; this date marks the transparent neon highlighting tool.
objects.funFact: Highlighter ink is bright but transparent, so you can still read the words underneath.

objects.name: Chalkboard
objects.kidDefinition: A dark board that lets teachers and children write with chalk and wipe it clean.
objects.dateBasis: James Pillans popularizes the large classroom slate chalkboard.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Small slates existed earlier; this date marks the shared classroom board.
objects.funFact: A teacher could show a whole class one large drawing instead of handing around many small slates.

objects.name: Vacuum flask
objects.kidDefinition: An insulated bottle that keeps drinks hot or cold for hours.
objects.dateBasis: Reinhold Burger patents and markets the Thermos vacuum flask.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Vacuum vessels existed in laboratories; this date marks the portable drink bottle.
objects.funFact: A vacuum layer slows heat moving between the drink and the outside air.

objects.name: Mechanical pencil
objects.kidDefinition: A pencil that pushes out thin graphite lead instead of being sharpened with a blade.
objects.dateBasis: The first clutch-style mechanical pencil is patented in Britain.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Graphite pencils are older; this date marks a refillable push-lead pencil.
objects.funFact: Mechanical pencils keep the writing point the same thickness as the lead moves forward.

objects.name: Toilet paper roll
objects.kidDefinition: Soft paper made in sheets or rolls for bathroom use.
objects.dateBasis: Joseph Gayetty sells packaged toilet paper in the United States.
objects.ambiguityNotes: People used many materials earlier; this date marks the packaged toilet-paper product.
objects.funFact: Early packaged toilet paper was sold as flat sheets before the familiar roll became standard.

objects.name: Electric washing machine
objects.kidDefinition: A powered machine that washes clothes in a spinning or tumbling tub.
objects.dateBasis: The Thor becomes one of the first commercially successful electric washing machines.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Hand washing and mechanical washers came earlier; this date marks the electric home appliance.
objects.funFact: Electric washers changed laundry from a day of scrubbing into a machine cycle.

objects.name: Internet
objects.kidDefinition: A worldwide network that lets computers and people share information.
objects.dateBasis: ARPANET adopts TCP/IP, a key foundation of the modern Internet.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier computer networks existed; this date marks the shared protocol foundation.
objects.funFact: The Internet is a network of networks, not one single giant computer.

objects.name: Text message
objects.kidDefinition: A short written message sent between mobile phones.
objects.dateBasis: Neil Papworth sends the first SMS text message.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Computer messaging existed earlier; this date marks the mobile-phone text message.
objects.funFact: The first text message said “Merry Christmas.”

objects.name: Nintendo
objects.kidDefinition: A game company known for consoles, characters, and video games.
objects.dateBasis: Fusajiro Yamauchi starts Nintendo as a playing-card company in Kyoto.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Nintendo made playing cards long before video games; this date marks the company’s founding.
objects.funFact: Nintendo began by making handmade playing cards, more than a century before the Nintendo Switch.

objects.name: Mickey Mouse
objects.kidDefinition: A cheerful cartoon mouse and one of the world’s most famous animated characters.
objects.dateBasis: Mickey Mouse debuts in the animated short Steamboat Willie.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The character appeared in an earlier silent cartoon; this date marks the famous sound-film debut.
objects.funFact: Mickey’s first famous film had synchronized sound, which helped make the character an instant star.

objects.name: Disneyland
objects.kidDefinition: A theme park where rides, stories, and characters fill a whole imagined world.
objects.dateBasis: Disneyland opens to visitors in Anaheim, California.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Amusement parks existed earlier; this date marks the modern story-themed destination park.
objects.funFact: Disneyland was designed as a place where families and children could explore stories together.

objects.name: Statue of Liberty
objects.kidDefinition: A giant statue in New York Harbor holding a torch and welcoming visitors.
objects.dateBasis: The Statue of Liberty is dedicated in New York Harbor.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the statue’s dedication and public unveiling, not the start of its design work.
objects.funFact: The statue arrived from France in pieces and was assembled on its island pedestal.

objects.name: Eiffel Tower
objects.kidDefinition: A tall iron landmark in Paris that visitors can climb for a view over the city.
objects.dateBasis: The Eiffel Tower opens to visitors at the Paris World’s Fair.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The tower was built for a temporary exhibition but became a lasting city landmark.
objects.funFact: More than 18,000 separate iron pieces fit together to make the tower’s famous shape.

objects.name: Golden Gate Bridge
objects.kidDefinition: A huge suspension bridge that carries traffic across the Golden Gate strait in San Francisco.
objects.dateBasis: The Golden Gate Bridge opens to pedestrians and vehicles.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier bridges existed elsewhere; this date marks the opening of this famous suspension bridge.
objects.funFact: Its tall towers and long cables help the bridge span a wide stretch of water.

objects.name: NASA
objects.kidDefinition: A space agency that explores Earth, the Moon, planets, and the universe.
objects.dateBasis: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration begins operations in the United States.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Rocket research came earlier; this date marks the NASA agency.
objects.funFact: NASA’s name stands for National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

objects.name: Hello Kitty
objects.kidDefinition: A friendly character created by Sanrio who appears on toys, stationery, and stories.
objects.dateBasis: Sanrio introduces Hello Kitty on a small coin purse in Japan.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The character’s global products expanded later; this date marks the first Hello Kitty product.
objects.funFact: Hello Kitty was first printed on a small coin purse before appearing on thousands of products.

objects.name: World Wide Web
objects.kidDefinition: The linked pages, pictures, and sites people visit through the Internet.
objects.dateBasis: Tim Berners-Lee proposes the World Wide Web at CERN.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The Internet’s network infrastructure came earlier; this date marks the web of linked pages on top of it.
objects.funFact: The first website explained what the World Wide Web was and how to use it.

objects.name: Piano
objects.kidDefinition: A keyboard instrument with strings that make notes when keys are pressed.
objects.dateBasis: Bartolomeo Cristofori develops the first piano in Italy.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier keyboard instruments existed; this date marks the hammer-and-string piano family.
objects.funFact: The piano was first called a gravicembalo col piano e forte, meaning soft and loud harpsichord.

objects.name: Electronic keyboard
objects.kidDefinition: An electronic instrument with piano-style keys that makes many different sounds.
objects.dateBasis: The Moog synthesizer and early electronic keyboards make keyboard-controlled electronic sound practical.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Electronic instruments came earlier; this date marks the modern keyboard-synthesizer family.
objects.funFact: An electronic keyboard can imitate a piano or create sounds that no acoustic instrument makes.

objects.name: Modern concrete
objects.kidDefinition: A hard building material made by mixing cement, water, and small pieces of stone or sand.
objects.dateBasis: Joseph Aspdin patents Portland cement, the key binder in modern concrete.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Concrete-like materials are ancient; this date marks the modern Portland-cement form.
objects.funFact: Concrete starts as a pourable mix and hardens into a stone-like material.

objects.name: Reinforced concrete
objects.kidDefinition: Concrete strengthened with steel bars or mesh so it can span and carry heavier loads.
objects.dateBasis: Joseph Monier patents reinforced concrete garden tubs and structures using iron reinforcement.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Concrete is older; this date marks the steel-reinforced form behind modern buildings and bridges.
objects.funFact: Concrete is strong when squeezed, while steel helps it resist pulling and bending.

objects.name: Umbrella
objects.kidDefinition: A portable canopy that helps keep rain or sun off your head and shoulders.
objects.dateBasis: Umbrella-like sunshades appear in ancient art and records in Asia and the Mediterranean.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The exact first umbrella is unknown; this date marks ancient portable sunshades.
objects.funFact: Early umbrellas were often made for shade and ceremony before they became everyday rain gear.

objects.name: Foldable umbrella
objects.kidDefinition: A compact umbrella with sections that fold down small enough to carry in a bag.
objects.dateBasis: Modern telescoping pocket umbrellas become widely available in the late 1960s.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Umbrellas are ancient; this date marks the compact folding form children recognize today.
objects.funFact: A folding umbrella uses sliding sections so a long canopy can fit inside a small case.

objects.name: Penicillin
objects.kidDefinition: A medicine made from a mold that can kill or stop many harmful bacteria.
objects.dateBasis: Alexander Fleming notices penicillin’s antibacterial effect.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The discovery came before mass production and hospital treatment; this date marks the discovery.
objects.funFact: Fleming noticed that bacteria would not grow close to a particular mold.

objects.name: Antibiotic treatment
objects.kidDefinition: Medicines that fight certain bacterial infections inside the body.
objects.dateBasis: Penicillin is first given as a widely reported life-saving treatment in a human patient.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Penicillin was discovered earlier; this date marks the beginning of practical antibiotic treatment.
objects.funFact: Antibiotics work against bacteria, but they do not cure illnesses caused by viruses such as colds.

objects.name: Volleyball
objects.kidDefinition: A team game where players keep a ball in the air and send it over a net.
objects.dateBasis: William G. Morgan invents a net game first called mintonette.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The rules changed over time; this date marks the game’s invention.
objects.funFact: The game was designed as a gentler indoor alternative to basketball for adults.

objects.name: Modern volleyball rules
objects.kidDefinition: The organized version of volleyball played with the familiar scoring, rotations, and team rules.
objects.dateBasis: Six-player teams and modern-style rules become standardized through YMCA volleyball.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The sport began in 1895; this date marks a later organized rules form.
objects.funFact: Volleyball changed from an open-ended recreation game into a fast team sport with fixed rotations.

objects.name: Swiffer
objects.kidDefinition: A lightweight cleaning tool with disposable cloths that pick up dust and dirt.
objects.dateBasis: Procter & Gamble launches the Swiffer cleaning system.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Mops and brooms are far older; this date marks the familiar disposable-cloth cleaning system.
objects.funFact: Swiffer cloths use tiny fibers that grab dust instead of simply pushing it around.

objects.name: Robot vacuum
objects.kidDefinition: A small round vacuum that drives around the floor and cleans by itself.
objects.dateBasis: iRobot launches the Roomba robot vacuum.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Vacuum cleaners are much older; this date marks the widely known self-driving home robot form.
objects.funFact: A robot vacuum uses sensors to notice walls, furniture, and edges of stairs.

objects.name: Insulated water bottle
objects.kidDefinition: A reusable bottle with special walls that help a drink stay cold or warm for hours.
objects.dateBasis: Hydro Flask helps popularize the modern colorful insulated reusable bottle.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Thermos bottles are older; this date marks the recent everyday reusable bottle trend.
objects.funFact: The airless space between the bottle’s walls slows heat from moving in or out.

objects.name: Air fryer
objects.kidDefinition: A countertop cooker that blows hot air around food to make it crisp.
objects.dateBasis: Philips introduces its Airfryer countertop appliance.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Convection ovens came earlier; this date marks the compact air fryer used in many kitchens today.
objects.funFact: An air fryer is really a very fast, small convection oven with a powerful fan.

objects.name: Video doorbell
objects.kidDefinition: A doorbell with a camera that lets people see and talk to a visitor from a phone.
objects.dateBasis: Ring launches a connected video doorbell for home use.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Doorbells and security cameras came earlier; this date marks the phone-connected front-door form.
objects.funFact: A video doorbell can send an alert even when nobody is home to hear the bell.

objects.name: Smart speaker
objects.kidDefinition: A speaker you can talk to for music, timers, questions, and some home controls.
objects.dateBasis: Amazon launches the Echo, helping establish the smart-speaker category.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Voice-recognition software and speakers came earlier; this date marks the familiar home smart speaker.
objects.funFact: A smart speaker uses microphones to hear a wake word from across a room.

objects.name: Crocs
objects.kidDefinition: Lightweight foam clogs with holes that people wear at the beach, pool, and around town.
objects.dateBasis: Crocs introduces its first Croslite foam shoe.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Clogs are much older; this date marks the colorful foam shoe style children recognize.
objects.funFact: The holes help water drain out and let air reach your feet.

objects.name: Heelys
objects.kidDefinition: Shoes with a removable wheel in the heel that lets a wearer roll along.
objects.dateBasis: Heelys begins selling wheeled shoes.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Roller skates are older; this date marks the shoe-with-a-hidden-wheel idea.
objects.funFact: A Heelys wheel sits in the heel, so the same shoe can walk or roll.

objects.name: Fitness tracker
objects.kidDefinition: A small wearable device that can count steps, track activity, and show movement goals.
objects.dateBasis: Fitbit launches one of the first widely used clip-on activity trackers.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Pedometers came earlier; this date marks the connected wearable tracker that syncs activity data.
objects.funFact: A fitness tracker can use a motion sensor to tell the difference between sitting and walking.

objects.name: Smartwatch
objects.kidDefinition: A wristwatch that can run apps, show messages, and track activity.
objects.dateBasis: Apple Watch launches as a widely recognized smartwatch.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Digital watches and earlier smartwatches existed; this date marks the app-based wearable form familiar today.
objects.funFact: A smartwatch can sense your wrist movement and gently tap to deliver a notification.

objects.name: Hot Pockets
objects.kidDefinition: A frozen stuffed sandwich that cooks quickly in a microwave.
objects.dateBasis: Hot Pockets begin appearing in stores as microwaveable stuffed sandwiches.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Filled pastries and sandwiches are older; this date marks the branded microwave snack form.
objects.funFact: Hot Pockets use a special sleeve to help the outside become crisp in a microwave.

objects.name: Bagel Bites
objects.kidDefinition: Small bagel halves topped like tiny pizzas and heated for a quick snack.
objects.dateBasis: Bagel Bites launches as a frozen mini-pizza snack.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Bagels and pizza are older; this date marks the frozen bite-size combination.
objects.funFact: Bagel Bites combine two familiar foods: a chewy bagel and a pizza topping.

objects.name: Lunchables
objects.kidDefinition: A ready-to-pack lunch kit with small crackers, cheese, meat, or other snack pieces.
objects.dateBasis: Kraft Heinz launches Lunchables as a packaged lunch kit.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Packed lunches are older; this date marks the mix-and-match branded lunch kit.
objects.funFact: Lunchables made it possible to build a little cracker sandwich right in a lunch tray.

objects.name: Fruit Gushers
objects.kidDefinition: Soft fruit snacks with a juicy center that bursts when you bite them.
objects.dateBasis: General Mills launches Fruit Gushers fruit snacks.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Fruit candy is older; this date marks the liquid-centered snack children recognize.
objects.funFact: The center is made to feel like a tiny splash of juice inside the chewy shell.

objects.name: Uncrustables
objects.kidDefinition: A sealed crustless sandwich with a filling such as peanut butter and jelly.
objects.dateBasis: The first sealed crustless sandwiches are produced for schools in Minnesota.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Peanut butter sandwiches are older; this date marks the sealed, frozen, crustless snack form.
objects.funFact: The crimped edge seals the filling inside so the sandwich has no loose crusts.

objects.name: Go-Gurt
objects.kidDefinition: Yogurt in a squeezeable tube that can be eaten without a spoon.
objects.dateBasis: General Mills launches Go-Gurt in the United States.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Yogurt is ancient; this date marks the tube-shaped grab-and-go yogurt snack.
objects.funFact: Go-Gurt was designed so yogurt could travel in a lunchbox without needing a bowl.

objects.name: Nintendo Entertainment System
objects.kidDefinition: A home game console that brought cartridge games such as Super Mario Bros. into many living rooms.
objects.dateBasis: Nintendo launches the NES in the United States.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Arcade games and the Japanese Famicom came earlier; this date marks the iconic North American home-console launch.
objects.funFact: The NES helped make home video games a regular part of family living rooms.

objects.name: American Girl dolls
objects.kidDefinition: Dolls with stories, outfits, and accessories that represent girls from different times and places.
objects.dateBasis: Pleasant Company introduces the first American Girl historical dolls.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Dolls are ancient; this date marks the story-rich American Girl doll collection.
objects.funFact: The first American Girl dolls came with books that told stories from each character’s time.

objects.name: Game Boy
objects.kidDefinition: A handheld game system that plays cartridges on a small screen.
objects.dateBasis: Nintendo launches the Game Boy in Japan.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Handheld electronic games came earlier; this date marks Nintendo’s cartridge-based Game Boy system.
objects.funFact: Game Boy games came on small cartridges that could be swapped in seconds.

objects.name: Polly Pocket
objects.kidDefinition: A tiny doll world that folds into a pocket-size case with miniature rooms and accessories.
objects.dateBasis: Bluebird Toys introduces the first Polly Pocket compact playsets.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Dollhouses are older; this date marks the miniature play world that closes into a compact case.
objects.funFact: Early Polly Pocket worlds were small enough to close up and carry like a little treasure case.

objects.name: Pokémon Trading Card Game
objects.kidDefinition: A card game where players collect Pokémon cards and use them in friendly battles.
objects.dateBasis: The Pokémon Trading Card Game launches in Japan.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Pokémon video games launched earlier that year; this date marks the first trading-card game release.
objects.funFact: A Pokémon card can be both a collectible picture and a piece in a strategy game.

objects.name: Furby
objects.kidDefinition: A fuzzy electronic toy that moves, talks, and reacts when children play with it.
objects.dateBasis: Tiger Electronics releases Furby.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Talking toys are older; this date marks the interactive furry creature toy craze.
objects.funFact: Furby first speaks a made-up language and gradually mixes in more English words.

objects.name: Beyblade
objects.kidDefinition: A spinning-top toy that players launch into a small arena for a spinning battle.
objects.dateBasis: Takara releases the first modern Beyblade spinning tops in Japan.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Spinning tops are ancient; this date marks the customizable battle-top toy line.
objects.funFact: Beyblade tops can be taken apart and rebuilt with different pieces for different moves.

objects.name: Bratz dolls
objects.kidDefinition: Fashion dolls with big personalities, bold clothes, and a group of close friends.
objects.dateBasis: MGA Entertainment launches the first Bratz dolls.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Fashion dolls are older; this date marks the Bratz character line.
objects.funFact: The first Bratz group had four friends: Yasmin, Cloe, Jade, and Sasha.

objects.name: Webkinz
objects.kidDefinition: A plush toy with a code that unlocked a matching virtual pet world online.
objects.dateBasis: Ganz launches Webkinz plush toys and the Webkinz World website.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Plush toys and online games existed earlier; this date marks the toy-and-website combination.
objects.funFact: Each Webkinz came with a secret code that let its owner care for a digital pet online.

objects.name: Nintendo Wii
objects.kidDefinition: A home game console with motion controllers that react when players swing, point, and move.
objects.dateBasis: Nintendo launches the Wii game console.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Motion games existed earlier; this date marks the Wii’s widely adopted motion-controller system.
objects.funFact: The Wii Remote made a living-room swing feel like a tennis shot or bowling throw on screen.

objects.name: Nintendo Switch
objects.kidDefinition: A game system that can play on a TV or travel as a handheld screen.
objects.dateBasis: Nintendo releases the Switch hybrid game console.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Home and handheld consoles came earlier; this date marks the system that easily changes between both ways to play.
objects.funFact: The Switch controllers can slide off the sides so two people can play together right away.

objects.name: Squishmallows
objects.kidDefinition: Round, soft plush toys made for hugging, collecting, and imaginative play.
objects.dateBasis: Kellytoy introduces the first Squishmallows plush characters.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Stuffed animals are much older; this date marks the round, marshmallow-soft character plush line.
objects.funFact: Squishmallows are filled with soft fiber that makes them feel more like a pillow than a traditional plush toy.
